scenarios.title: The Outdoor Store
scenarios.narrativeText: You and four friends are at a large outdoor store one week before a two-week, unmapped mountain expedition. The group has finished buying the basics, but the money is gone. You have one final $500 store credit to spend. Your friends are all over the place, arguing about what to grab for the trip. You have the final say on what goes into the cart.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You're holding the $500 credit. What are you pushing the group to buy?

options.label: A
options.title: The Hiking Upgrade
options.text: You grab professional-grade hiking boots and carbon-fiber trekking poles for yourself. You tell the group, "If I'm going to handle the terrain and set the pace, I need to know my feet are going to hold up no matter what."

options.label: B
options.title: The Woodsman's Kit
options.text: You pick up a high-capacity expedition pack with an integrated frame and a heavy-duty, razor-sharp camp axe. You tell the group, "We need to be able to carry serious weight and process whatever we find out there. This axe is going to do a lot of work."

options.label: C
options.title: The Recovery Setup
options.text: You load up on a high-end, lightweight cot and a premium sleeping system. You tell the group, "I don't care how tough we act, if we don't get deep, restorative sleep, we're going to be useless by day three. We need to recover properly."

options.label: D
options.title: The Kitchen & Sustainment Reserve
options.text: You fill the cart with a top-tier, redundant stove system, extra fuel, and a crate of high-density rations. You tell the group, "We can deal with a lot, but we aren't going to be worth a damn if we don't have good fuel and hot food to keep us going."

scenarios.title: The Ridge, the Brush, or the Bog
scenarios.narrativeText: It is late afternoon on day two of your expedition, and you need to reach the designated basecamp on the other side of a steep, rugged mountain ridge before nightfall. The direct trail is blocked, leaving you with three distinct paths to get to the exact same destination. To the left, you can take the established valley trail that winds completely around the base of the ridge; it is safe and easy, but it adds two full hours to the march, guaranteeing you will be navigating the final stretch in pitch darkness. Straight ahead, a steep scramble goes directly over the rocky crest; it is the most direct route, but the terrain is incredibly rough, requiring intense physical exertion on loose shale. To the right, a low-lying wetland route cuts along the edge of the lake; it is flat and fast, but the thick brush and deep water mean wading through heavy mud, risking wet gear and hypothermia as the temperature drops.
scenarios.decisionPoint: With daylight fading and the same destination waiting on the other side, which route do you commit the team to take?

options.label: A
options.title: The Low-Risk Contour
options.text: You choose the long route around the base of the mountain. You argue that keeping your footing on an easy trail is worth burning two extra hours, accepting that the team will have to pitch camp using headlamps in the dark to avoid injury or wet gear.

options.label: B
options.title: The Ridge Scramble
options.text: You choose the direct route straight over the rough, rocky crest. You argue that taking the high ground keeps the team dry and beats the sunset, betting that the group has the raw physical strength to push through the punishing vertical climb.

options.label: C
options.title: The Wetland Cut
options.text: You choose the fast route through the low-lying bog. You argue that speed is your best asset to beat the cold, deciding that clearing the thick brush and taking a direct path is worth the risk of getting bogged down in wet mud.

options.label: D
options.title: The Safe Bivouac
options.text: You refuse to rush the mountain, calling a halt to pitch camp right where you are on the near side. You argue that forcing a tired team through dark trails, rough rocks, or cold water just to reach a specific spot is a trap, choosing instead to conserve your energy and cross safely in the morning.

scenarios.title: The Camp Footprint
scenarios.narrativeText: It is the end of day three, and the team has successfully reached a flat, heavily wooded clearing to establish a semi-permanent basecamp for the next few days. The site is good, but the physical environment presents clear trade-offs in how you arrange your camp footprint as a light drizzle starts and the wind picks up. Your friends are already dropping their packs, exhausted and eager to rest. You need to assign the immediate priorities for setting up before total darkness sets in. One area sits close to a fast-moving stream, offering easy water access that simplifies daily operations but requires significant upfront effort to secure against the weather. Another area is tucked deep under a thick canopy of dead-standing timber, which blocks the rain completely but poses a falling branch hazard if the wind worsens. A third spot is a clean, open rock shelf—perfectly safe from falling limbs but entirely exposed to the elements.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Looking at the clearing as the temperature drops, how do you direct the group to establish the camp?

options.label: A
options.title: The Efficiency Core
options.text: You order everyone to concentrate all energy on pitching tents immediately on the open rock shelf, exposed to the weather but clear of hazards. You argue that getting shelter up fast is the highest priority, and you can deal with the wind as long as everyone is dry and secure from falling timber.

options.label: B
options.title: The Infrastructure Model
options.text: You direct the team to invest their remaining energy into securing the stream location, building out structural windbreaks and a stable perimeter right next to your primary water source. You argue that securing an optimal, long-term resource spot is worth the heavy upfront effort to make operations seamless for the next three days.

options.label: C
options.title: The Recovery Focus
options.text: You pitch camp deep under the thick timber canopy to take immediate advantage of the natural rain shield. You argue that conserving the group's remaining physical energy and staying out of the drizzle outweighs the statistical risk of a falling limb, prioritizing immediate comfort and recovery.

options.label: D
options.title: The Specialist Protocol
options.text: You assign each person complete responsibility for a distinct domain—water collection, shelter setup, fire preparation, or food storage. Rather than forcing everyone into a single centralized footprint, you allow each member to establish their workspace where they believe it will function best, arguing that decentralized ownership and individual autonomy create a more resilient camp.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Thunder
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 2:00 AM on night three. The light drizzle from earlier has steadily built into a heavy, thundering downpour that echoes through the mountain valley. Lightning flashes in the distance, illuminating the camp through the tent walls, and a steady wind is testing your knots. Everyone is awake, listening to the weather crackling and thundering in the sky above. Inside your shelter, you notice that water has begun to saturate the ground outside, and a slow drip is starting to form over one of the gear storage piles. Your friends are calling out between shelters, checking on each other, and wondering if they need to get up and adjust the camp layout before the storm gets worse.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Listening to the storm hit the shelters in the dark, how do you handle the group's reaction to the weather?

options.label: A
options.title: The Stay-Put Order
options.text: You tell everyone to stay zipped inside their shelters and ride it out. You argue that getting out into the cold rain to fix minor leaks is a classic mistake that just gets people wet and shivering, betting that your basic shelter setups will hold until morning.

options.label: B
options.title: The Trenching Detail
options.text: You get out with a flashlight to dig drainage channels around the low-lying areas of the camp and secure the gear line. You argue that letting water pool early creates a cascading mess for the next two days, choosing to put in the uncomfortable midnight maintenance work to protect the footprint.

options.label: C
options.title: The Welfare Check
options.text: You open up your shelter to check on the rest of the team, passing extra dry layers to anyone dealing with a leak. You argue that keeping tabs on everyone's morale and thermal comfort during a rough night is the highest priority, ensuring nobody is quietly freezing or panicking in the dark.

options.label: D
options.title: The Individual Status
options.text: You shout back that everyone needs to assess and manage their own immediate shelter footprint. You argue that trying to coordinate a group effort in a midnight downpour is useless, leaving it to each individual to handle their own leaks and secure their personal gear.

scenarios.title: The Compromised Canopy
scenarios.narrativeText: It is now 3:00 AM on night three, and the downpour shows no signs of slowing down. Inside your own shelter, you realize the fabric is completely saturated. There is a well-known reality with single-wall tents: the moment you start touching the wet fabric or moving gear around, you break the surface tension, causing the water to actively seep through and compromise the dryness of your entire space. At the same time, you look out the mesh door and notice the communal supply tarp—where the bulk of the group's food and cooking gear is stored—is beginning to sag heavily under a massive pocket of pooled water. Opening your tent door to fix it means letting the driving rain flood your own dry clothes, but leaving it alone risks a total failure of the food shelter.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Trapped between protecting your personal dry environment and securing the shared supply line, what do you do?

options.label: A
options.title: The Static Defensive
options.text: You keep your tent zipped tight and refuse to touch the saturated walls, staying perfectly still to preserve your immediate personal dryness. You argue that maintaining your own thermal baseline is your primary duty, and ruining your own gear to save a sagging tarp in the dark creates two problems instead of one.

options.label: B
options.title: The Exposure Intervention
options.text: You unzip your tent, step out into the downpour, and quickly clear the pooling water off the food tarp before it collapses. You accept that your personal clothes and shelter will get wet, arguing that protecting the collective food supply from a catastrophic soaking is worth the immediate sacrifice of your own comfort.

options.label: C
options.title: The Coordinated Attempt
options.text: You call out to the closest shelter, trying to coordinate a quick, synchronized push from the inside of their own vestibules to nudge the tarp frame. You accept that blind coordination in a midnight storm is highly uncertain and might fail before the tarp gives way, but you argue that attempting a collective fix is better than rushing out or doing nothing.

options.label: D
options.title: The Calculated Containment
options.text: You stay inside your tent but use a trekking pole to carefully rearrange your personal gear away from your own walls without touching the fabric. You shout to the group to monitor their own supplies, arguing that each person must focus on stabilizing what is within their reach rather than launching a risky midnight salvage operation.

scenarios.title: The Morning After
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 7:00 AM on morning four. The storm has finally passed, leaving the mountain valley quiet, damp, and freezing cold. As the team crawls out of their shelters, the reality of the night sets in: everyone is exhausted, several sleeping bags are damp, and morale has bottomed out. The immediate task is to get the camp functional, pack up, and prepare for the day's hike. However, energy is low and people are moving slowly, shivering as they try to reorganize. To get the group moving and warm, you need to establish the very first priority of the morning. One option is to immediately build a large, high-energy campfire to dry out gear and raise spirits, though finding dry wood after a downpour will take a concentrated group effort. Another option is to bypass a fire entirely and force everyone to pack their wet gear immediately, using the heavy physical exertion of the march itself to generate body heat and make up for lost time.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Standing in the damp, freezing morning camp with a shivering team, how do you direct the first hour of the day?

options.label: A
options.title: The Momentum Surge
options.text: You order the group to skip the fire, pack up the damp camp immediately, and get moving on the trail. You argue that sitting around in wet gear waiting for a fire to catch is a trap that breeds stagnation, choosing instead to use the raw physical exertion of hiking to naturally warm the team and clear the valley.

options.label: B
options.title: The Thermal Restoration
options.text: You halt all packing and mobilize the entire team to hunt for dry standing wood and resinous pine knots to build a massive fire. You argue that forcing people to march while shivering and damp is an operational risk, betting that burning an hour of daylight to dry gear and restore core body heat is an essential investment.

options.label: C
options.title: The Metabolic Priority
options.text: You direct all immediate energy toward boiling water on the stable camp stoves to distribute hot coffee and high-calorie rations while everyone remains in their shelters. You argue that internal heat and metabolic fueling must come before either heavy physical labor or trail packing, focusing on re-centering the team's internal comfort first.

options.label: D
options.title: The Parallel Prep
options.text: You refuse to set a single uniform task, telling the team to divide and conquer based on their immediate state—those who are dry start packing group gear, while those who are wet focus entirely on drying out their personal kits. You recognize that self-directed work will likely create inefficiencies, duplicated effort, and uneven standards across the camp, but you accept those costs to give individuals the flexibility to self-correct.

scenarios.title: The Distribution of Weight
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 9:00 AM on day four, and the team is finally packed up and ready to move. However, the midnight storm has left behind a structural problem: three of the group's four-person tents are completely waterlogged, adding an extra eight pounds of dead, saturated weight to each one. This extra group gear must be carried out, but your teammates are starting the day at completely different physical baselines. Two members are visibly exhausted from a sleepless night and shivering, while the other two managed to stay dry and are full of nervous energy. The heavy, wet tents are currently sitting on the ground, and you need to decide how to distribute this uneven burden before the first mile begins.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Looking at the wet gear and the varying physical states of your team, how do you assign the load?

options.label: A
options.title: The Absolute Equality
options.text: You divide the extra wet weight mathematically down to the ounce, ensuring every single person carries an identical share of the communal burden. You argue that on a team expedition, true solidarity means sharing the pain equally, refusing to let individual performance variances dictate a deviation from uniform standards.

options.label: B
options.title: The Capability Load
options.text: You assign all the heavy, waterlogged tents to the two dry, fresh team members, leaving the exhausted members with only their personal kits. You argue that leadership requires maximizing systemic efficiency, protecting your vulnerable assets by leveraging the temporary strength of those who are currently at 100%.

options.label: C
options.title: The Collective Rotation
options.text: You keep the original gear assignments but implement a strict, mandatory time-based rotation, forcing the group to drop packs and swap the heavy wet tents between every single member every sixty minutes. You argue that a rotating burden keeps any one person from burning out entirely, prioritizing long-term group endurance over smooth, continuous pacing.

options.label: D
options.title: The Autonomy Auction
options.text: You place the wet gear in the center and allow the team to self-select their loads, accepting that some people may underestimate their limits, overestimate their willingness, or quietly avoid the heaviest burdens. You argue that forcing assignments onto adults breaks trust, choosing to protect individual agency even if it results in an uneven or sluggish operation.

scenarios.title: The Pacing Tension
scenarios.narrativeText: It is noon on day four. With the heavy, wet gear distributed, the team has been marching uphill for three hours. The physical division from this morning is now manifesting on the trail as a severe pacing gap. The two fresh, dry team members are moving at an aggressive clip, pulling far ahead and waiting at trail bends, visibly annoyed by the delays. Meanwhile, the two exhausted team members are lagging significantly behind, stopping frequently to adjust their straps and catch their breath. The distance between the front and the back of your line is widening dangerously, stretching out over a quarter-mile of dense, winding mountain trail where sightlines are poor. You are walking in the middle of the gap, and you need to set the pacing strategy for the rest of the afternoon.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Standing between a fractured line as the distance between your front and rear runners widens, how do you handle the team's pace?

options.label: A
options.title: The Lead Pace
options.text: You command the front runners to maintain their fast speed and tell the lagging members to push their limits to keep up. You argue that slowing down the entire collective unit to match the weakest link burns precious daylight and destroys the momentum needed to clear the ridge before dark.

options.label: B
options.title: The Anchor Consolidation
options.text: You halt the front runners completely and force them to match the exact pace of the slowest, most exhausted members, keeping the entire team in a tight, single file behind the anchor. You argue that a team is only as fast as its slowest member, prioritizing absolute group cohesion and safety over speed.

options.label: C
options.title: The Leapfrog Interval
options.text: You instruct the fast front runners to push ahead to a designated landmark one mile out, drop their packs to rest, and then hike back empty-handed to take the heavy gear from the lagging members. You recognize that the repeated backtracking will consume additional energy from your strongest members and may leave them exhausted later in the day, but you argue that using excess capacity to actively buffer struggling units maximizes your total systemic throughput.

options.label: D
options.title: The Split-Unit Autonomy
options.text: You divide the group into two independent pairs—the fast group moves ahead to set up the next camp early, while you stay behind to manage the slow group at their own comfortable rhythm. You recognize that splitting the team reduces your immediate communication and leaves the trailing group without full camp setup support, but you accept that risk to eliminate interpersonal frustration and let each unit move naturally.

scenarios.title: The Private Stash
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 4:00 PM on day four, and the team has dropped packs at a trail junction for a brief afternoon break. The mood is a bit quiet and road-weary, but stable. While everyone is digging out the standard, uninspiring bulk trail mix from the shared food bags, one team member unzips a side pocket and pulls out a premium energy bar and a specialized sports drink they brought from home. It's nothing major, but it wasn't part of the shared spreadsheet everyone contributed to before the trip. A couple of your teammates notice the upgrade, and while nobody says anything out loud, there is a distinct shift in the air as people watch them snap the bar in half.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Noticing the minor social friction over unpooled personal items, how do you view the situation?

options.label: A
options.title: The Individual Prep
options.text: You ignore the looks and support the member eating their snack. You argue that personal foresight and individual preference are entirely their own business, and if people wanted premium snacks on the trail, they should have packed them in their personal gear before leaving.

options.label: B
options.title: The Unified Standard
options.text: You casually suggest that next time, all specialty items should go into the group pool so everyone eats the same tier of rations. You argue that keeping everyone on an identical standard prevents subtle divisions and maintains a consistent, shared experience across the line.

options.label: C
options.title: The Informal Bridge
options.text: You use the moment to jokingly ask the member if they're willing to trade a bite of the bar for a handful of trail mix, breaking the ice naturally. You recognize that inserting yourself with a joke risks making the moment awkward or drawing even more unwanted attention to the disparity if the humor lands poorly, but you argue that a casual trade is the best way to defuse the tension without creating a formal issue.

options.label: D
options.title: The Mind-Your-Own Policy
options.text: You keep your head down, focus entirely on re-tying your boots, and stay completely out of it. You argue that policing what people eat or how others react to it is a waste of leadership energy, leaving adults to manage their own personal boundaries and trail habits independently.

scenarios.title: The Blind Fork
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 5:30 PM on day four. The approaching storm front hits the ridge earlier than expected, bringing sudden fog and a driving rain that drops visibility down to twenty feet. Because of the pacing differences earlier, your two fastest members pushed hard to outrace the weather and have completely vanished into the mist ahead. You are walking with the trailing group when the trail hits an unmarked, muddy fork in the dense woods. There is no cell service, the wind is howling too loudly for shouting to work, and you can't tell which path the forward pair took. Pushing forward blindly risks completely separating the two halves of the team in a storm, but halting in the exposed downpour to wait or search will leave everyone freezing.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Standing at a blind fork in a worsening storm with a fractured team, how do you handle the navigation?

options.label: A
options.title: The Fixed Rendezvous
options.text: You pick the path that looks most established on your map and push the trailing group forward down it to the lake, trusting the forward pair to do the same. You argue that in a storm, everyone must independently execute the original plan and move toward the final objective rather than hesitating at intermediate points.

options.label: B
options.title: The Hard Anchor
options.text: You order the trailing group to halt completely at the fork, pitch an emergency tarp right where you are, and stay put until the forward pair realizes they lost you and hikes back. You argue that maintaining a known, fixed location is the absolute rule of search and rescue, prioritizing team re-consolidation over trail progress.

options.label: C
options.title: The Active Scout
options.text: You have the trailing group wait under a tree while you drop your pack and jog a few hundred yards down both paths to look for fresh footprints or broken branches before making a group move. You recognize that splitting yourself from the trailing group in zero visibility carries a high risk of getting disoriented or losing valuable time, but you argue it is the only way to make an informed decision.

options.label: D
options.title: The Trail Marker
options.text: You pick a path, leave a clear, makeshift arrow out of rocks or branches at the fork for anyone behind you, and continue forward. You argue that creating highly visible navigation cues for the route is more valuable than freezing in place or conducting a blind search, trusting decentralized recovery over forced tracking.

scenarios.title: The Pre-Empted Campsite
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 6:45 PM on day four. The trailing group has finally made it down to the lake basin, and to your immense relief, you have successfully reunited with the forward pair. However, the storm has created a new, immediate bottleneck: the lake basin is heavily flooded, leaving only one small, elevated gravel shelf dry enough to pitch the group's remaining intact tents. The problem is that another independent hiking group of three people arrived from the opposite direction just ten minutes before you did. They are currently shivering in the downpour, unpacking their gear, and preparing to lay claim to the exact same dry shelf. There is physically not enough room on this high ground for both groups' setups, and the surrounding low-lying areas are rapidly turning into ankle-deep mud puddles.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Arriving at the only viable camp real estate to find another party staking a claim, how do you manage the space?

options.label: A
options.title: The Prior Claim
options.text: You immediately march up to the other group, explain that your team has been tracking toward this specific site all day, and assertively stake your claim to the premium dry ground. You argue that your team's size, exposure level, and physical exhaustion require you to secure the best defensive position possible, refusing to yield critical structural safety out of politeness.

options.label: B
options.title: The Complete Yield
options.text: You immediately concede the dry shelf to the other group without a dispute and direct your team to start pitching your tents in the muddy, low-lying zone. You argue that entering into a territorial conflict with strangers during a storm introduces severe social risk and chaos, choosing to absorb the physical discomfort of a wet campsite to maintain absolute ethical boundaries and peace.

options.label: C
options.title: The Compressed Share
options.text: You approach their leader and propose a tightly packed compromise: both groups condense their tent footprints, overlap rainflies, and crowd together to fit all the shelters onto the single dry shelf. You recognize that losing physical separation and mixing camp spaces with strangers will create an cramped, highly inefficient environment for the night, but you argue it minimizes total human exposure.

options.label: D
options.title: The Alternative Search
options.text: You bypass the shelf entirely, keep your packs on, and immediately push your team another half-mile down an unverified side trail into the woods to find a completely separate clearing. You argue that staying to fight over or crowd into a single site is a high-friction trap, choosing to maintain your unit's total autonomy even if it means marching longer in the dark.

scenarios.title: The Neighbor's Request
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 7:30 PM on day four. The shelters are finally pitched, and the reality of camping in close proximity to the other three-person hiking group has set in. Whether sharing the tight gravel shelf or pitched just within sight in the woods, your camps are structurally entangled. As the rain settles into a steady drizzle, the leader of the other group walks over to your perimeter. They explain that during their frantic scramble to beat the storm, they dropped and broke their only folding camp shovel, and their water filtration system is running incredibly slow due to a clogged filter. They ask if they can borrow your group's primary trowel to dig their sanitation trenches and use your gravity-fed water filter to process their evening supply.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Facing a neighboring unit requesting access to your team's essential operational gear, how do you manage your resources?

options.label: A
options.title: The Strict Isolation
options.text: You politely but firmly decline their request, stating that your team's gear must remain exclusively within your camp for the night. You argue that lending out essential, high-wear infrastructure like filters and sanitation tools during a multi-day trip introduces an unacceptable risk of equipment breakage or contamination, prioritizing absolute self-reliance.

options.label: B
options.title: The Open Commons
options.text: You immediately hand over both the trowel and the water filter, telling them to keep the gear for as long as they need it tonight. You argue that in the backcountry, all human assets must pool together during a crisis, choosing to accept the wear-and-tear risks to establish an absolute baseline of cross-camp community and mutual aid.

options.label: C
options.title: The Monopolized Service
options.text: You decline to let the equipment leave your sight, but you offer a compromise: you or one of your members will personally go over to filter their water for them and dig the necessary trench lines. You recognize that donating your team's physical labor after an exhausting day will heavily drain your members' remaining energy, but you argue it fulfills a moral obligation while keeping total physical custody of your assets.

options.label: D
options.title: The Transactional Barter
options.text: You agree to lend them the water filter and trowel, but only if they agree to trade something of equal value for the evening—such as a dry bundles of fire-starter wood or a portion of their specialized weather maps. You argue that structural relationships between independent units function best on clear, reciprocal transactions rather than free compliance or top-down charity.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Boundary
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 2:00 AM on night four. The rain has stopped, but the temperature has plummeted, leaving the camp quiet and frozen. You are shaken awake by a team member who points out through the tent mesh: a lone member of the neighboring camp is currently crossing your perimeter with a headlamp, heading directly toward the tarp where your group's specialized ropes and technical packs are stored. In the pitch black, it is impossible to tell if they are simply disoriented, looking to borrow a tool without asking, or sorting through your gear. The rest of your team is fast asleep, and you have only seconds to react before the person steps into your central gear pile.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Spotting a neighboring camper crossing your perimeter toward your critical assets in the dark, how do you engage?

options.label: A
options.title: The Firm Command
options.text: You immediately un-zip the tent, step outside, shine your flashlight at them, and firmly tell them to stop where they are. You argue that establishing an immediate, unyielding boundary prevents any ambiguity from turning into an incident, choosing to use a strong deterrent to protect your assets even if it risks embarrassing an innocent person.

options.label: B
options.title: The Quiet Shadow
options.text: You slip out of your shelter silently into the darkness without turning on a light, tracking their movements closely from the shadows to see exactly what they do before making your presence known. You recognize that waiting to gather undeniable evidence of their intent means they may have enough time to access, damage, or remove critical gear before you can stop them, but you argue that moving prematurely destroys your information advantage.

options.label: C
options.title: The De-escalating Greeting
options.text: You call out warmly and casually from inside the safety of your tent, asking them if they are lost or if they need help finding their way back to their shelters. You recognize that giving an unknown actor the benefit of the doubt inside your perimeter risks lowering your guard against a bad actor, but you argue it prevents a hostile, dangerous misunderstanding in the dark.

options.label: D
options.title: The Group Awakening
options.text: You stay low inside the shelter, shake your resting teammates awake to quietly alert them, and form a coordinated line before stepping out together. You recognize that taking the time to wake and organize your sleeping team causes a distinct operational delay that might allow the individual to slip away or handle your gear unhindered, but you accept that cost to ensure you have full collective support and security before a confrontation.

scenarios.title: The Morning Disclosure
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 7:00 AM on day five. The midnight incident has passed, and as the group prepares breakfast, the leader of the neighboring camp walks into your clearing. They look exhausted and genuinely apologetic, explaining that their teammate who crossed your perimeter last night was severely dehydrated, sleep-deprived, and looking for their own group's water storage bag in a state of confusion. To show goodwill, their leader offers to let your group use their highly detailed, local topographic map coordinates for the upcoming ridge cross—a resource that would let you bypass a notoriously steep, muddy boulder field on today's route. However, you notice that their team is now completely out of fuel canisters, meaning they will have to eat cold, uncooked rations for the remaining three days of their trip unless someone gives them a spare.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Offered a highly valuable navigational asset by a struggling neighbor who clearly needs your team's mechanical resources, how do you handle the exchange?

options.label: A
options.title: The Transactional Swap
options.text: You accept their topographic coordinates, but only after explicitly offering one of your group's spare fuel canisters in return. You argue that clear, equal reciprocity maintains clean structural boundaries between independent units, refusing to accept high-value favors without paying a fair, balanced price.

options.label: B
options.title: The Free Advantage
options.text: You gladly take their map coordinates to optimize your route, thank them warmly for their generosity, but keep your spare fuel canisters securely inside your packs without offering them. You argue that your primary duty is to maximize your own team's resource cushion, using their voluntary goodwill to get ahead without exposing your own inventory to depletion.

options.label: C
options.title: The Generous Assistance
options.text: You give them a spare fuel canister immediately to ensure they can cook hot meals, but you decline to take their topographic coordinates, choosing to stick strictly to your original trail route. You argue that helping a vulnerable neighbor is an absolute human obligation, but you choose to remain entirely self-reliant for your own path rather than changing plans based on outside data.

options.label: D
options.title: The Complete Disengagement
options.text: You politely decline their map coordinates and keep your fuel canisters to yourself, ending the conversation quickly so your team can focus on packing up. You argue that mixing inventories, trading resources, or altering routes with outside parties on day five introduces unpredictable variables and dependencies, choosing total operational isolation.

scenarios.title: The Shared Chimney
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 11:30 AM on day five. Having coordinated your departure from camp together this morning, your group and the neighboring three-person team are moving as a combined five-mile-per-hour convoy. You have reached the base of the high mountain pass—a steep, single-file scramble through a treacherous rock chimney where a single misstep can cause a severe fall. As the combined line moves upward, the external team's dehydrated member freezes on a vertical ledge, completely paralyzed by exhaustion and fear. Because the two groups are physically interlinked on the narrow route, this failure instantly stalls the entire column. You are exposed to bitter winds on a steep face, your timeline is evaporating, and you need to resolve the deadlock.
scenarios.decisionPoint: With a combined column stalled on an exposed rock face due to an external partner's failure, how do you manage the bottleneck?

options.label: A
options.title: The Assertive Overtake
options.text: You direct your team members to carefully climb around the stalled hiker, step over the gap, and continue up the ridge to clear the bottleneck. You argue that your primary duty is to your own group's timeline and safety, and trapping high-performing assets behind a partner's localized collapse invites unnecessary risk for your people.

options.label: B
options.title: The Integrated Rescue
options.text: You push to the front of the stalled gap yourself, offer to shoulder the frozen hiker's pack, and have your team form a human spotting line to physically guide their feet up the rock face. You recognize that absorbing their dead weight and exposure risk heavily strains your own team's physical reserve, but you argue that an integrated column requires integrated accountability to get through.

options.label: C
options.title: The Secure Retreat
options.text: You order your team to systematically climb backward down the rock face to a secure, wider ledge below, dropping your packs to wait until the other group manages to clear the obstacle on their own. You argue that crowding a panicked climber on a technical ascent creates a dangerous psychological pressure cooker, choosing to sacrifice a major block of daylight to maintain a safe, clean separation.

options.label: D
options.title: The Technical Detour
options.text: You pull your team completely off the established route and commit to an unmaintained, loose scree slope to the left to bypass the chimney entirely. You recognize that navigating an unverified gravel field carries a significantly higher risk of an immediate ankle injury, but you accept that physical risk to break the alliance and regain total operational independence.

scenarios.title: The Divided Descent
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 2:30 PM on day five. The intense scramble over the pass is behind you, and the combined column has reached the high plateau where the trail splits for the long descent. The left fork is a steep, rugged drop through a creek bed—it is fast and direct, but punishing on knees and heavy packs. The right fork is a beautifully graded, gentle switchback trail that adds an extra four miles to the journey. The other group's leader notes that because their exhausted hiker spent their absolute last reserves of strength pushing through the chimney with your team, they cannot physically handle the jarring drops of the creek bed and must take the long switchbacks. Furthermore, taking that four-mile detour means they will be caught out after dark without any remaining fuel or hot food. Your own team is highly capable and eager to take the fast route to secure a camp before freezing temperatures set in.
scenarios.decisionPoint: With the shared crisis resolved but your partner heavily compromised by the joint effort, how do you manage the split?

options.label: A
options.title: The Clean Off-Ramp
options.text: You bid the other group farewell, take your team down the fast creek bed, and let them proceed down the switchbacks alone. You argue that the structural alliance was strictly for the ridge crossing, and once the bottleneck is cleared, a high-performing unit must reclaim its own speed and safety rather than inheriting an external group's long-term liabilities.

options.label: B
options.title: The Alliance Continuity
options.text: You keep your entire team locked into the combined column, committing everyone to the slow, four-mile switchback detour to escort them all the way down. You argue that because their member exhausted themselves keeping pace with the shared line, you have a lingering structural obligation to ensure they reach the valley safely, prioritizing relationship equity over your own timeline.

options.label: C
options.title: The Resource Fractionalization
options.text: You split your own team—letting your two fastest members take the rapid creek bed to secure your next campsite early, while you and your remaining member hike the long switchbacks with the other group. You recognize that fracturing your unit across two different sides of the mountain severely weakens your internal communication and emergency support capabilities, but you argue it balances internal efficiency with external obligation.

options.label: D
options.title: The Single-Standard Drag
options.text: You insist that both teams must stay together but force the entire column down the fast, rugged creek bed, ordering your strongest members to physically carry the neighbor's heavy gear packs to make it possible for their slow hiker. You argue that keeping all human assets unified on the most direct operational path is the only logical choice, choosing to absorb a massive immediate physical strain to prevent a total separation.

scenarios.title: The Inventory Reconciliation
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 8:30 AM on day six. The descent is behind you, and your team is preparing for the final, twenty-mile push toward the expedition's exit trailhead. As you pull your gear apart to pack up, you discover that a mistake was made during the chaotic, dark reorganization at the plateau yesterday: your team inadvertently packed the neighboring group's high-end, lightweight personal satellite communicator into one of your side pockets, while they mistakenly walked away with your team's heavy, baseline backup radio. You now possess a significantly superior communication asset that isn't yours, while they are stuck with an inferior tool. Turning around to hike back and find them to swap the gear back will cost your team an entire morning of daylight, forcing you to finish the trek in a treacherous canyon after dark.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Discovering an accidental gear swap that leaves your team with a superior asset but delays your schedule if corrected, how do you handle the inventory?

options.label: A
options.title: The Operational Keepsake
options.text: You slip the superior satellite communicator into your pack, keep moving forward on schedule, and decide to contact the other group to return it only after you have safely finished the expedition. You argue that maintaining your immediate timeline and safety margin overrides a non-critical asset correction on the trail, prioritizing immediate operational momentum over strict property boundaries.

options.label: B
options.title: The Immediate Reversal
options.text: You halt the entire team, drop packs, and turn around to hike back up the trail until you locate the other group to swap the gear back immediately. You argue that operating with property that is not yours destroys your team's ethical integrity, choosing to absorb a massive time deficit and a hazardous night-hike to ensure absolute equity and clean boundaries.

options.label: C
options.title: The Delayed Courier
options.text: You pick your two fastest, unburdened members and send them sprinting backward up the trail to find the other group and make the swap, while you and the remaining members continue walking slowly forward with the heavy gear. You recognize that splitting your team on the final leg reduces your immediate safety net and fractures your unit's collective strength, but you argue it is the only way to correct the mistake without stopping the line.

options.label: D
options.title: The Fixed Depository
options.text: You leave their satellite communicator inside a weatherproof bag hanging directly from a prominent, marked trail signpost right where you are, hoping they notice the swap and look for it, while you keep moving forward. You argue that you are not responsible for tracking down another group's assets, choosing a passive, systemic compromise that clears your hands of the gear without sacrificing your timeline.

scenarios.title: The Compressed Margin
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 1:30 PM on day six. Your team is moving through a deep river gorge on the final ten-mile leg toward the trailhead when a park ranger coming down the trail flags you down. They explain that an upstream dam release has been moved forward and a flood surge is expected to enter the gorge later this afternoon. Based on your current pace, your safety margin is extremely tight. Beating the water will require pushing the team significantly harder than planned, while delaying could leave you exposed inside the gorge.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Faced with a narrowing safety margin and an approaching flood surge, how do you execute the final leg of the expedition?

options.label: A
options.title: The Forced Redline
options.text: Ditch all non-essential group gear (stoves, heavy tools, extra tarps) right on the trail and break into an aggressive power-march. You argue that abandoning physical assets is a necessary cost to maximize immediate velocity and beat a hard deadline.

options.label: B
options.title: The High-Stain Hold
options.text: Keep packs fully loaded, lock into a tight file, and demand the team endure the grueling, high-speed pace together without stopping. You argue that stripping your inventory leaves you dangerously exposed if you fail to beat the water anyway.

options.label: C
options.title: The Tiered Extraction
options.text: Transfer the heaviest gear from your two weakest hikers to the two strongest, and order the unburdened group to move at an elevated, aggressive pace. You argue that asymmetrically overloading your peak performers balances team safety with asset preservation.

options.label: D
options.title: The Calculated Delay
options.text: Reject the race entirely. Halt the team, turn back a quarter-mile to an elevated rock outcrop, and prepare to bivouac for twelve hours until the flood crest subsides. You argue that racing a hard environmental clock in a choke point is an unacceptable gamble.

scenarios.title: The Upper Escarpment
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 3:30 PM on day six. Your team has clawed its way up the slick, muddy paths of the gorge, escaping the rising floodwaters below. While you are above the high-water mark, the terrain is an unstable mix of wet clay and loose shale. The exit is two miles away, but the trail is washed out by a fresh mudslide, leaving a forty-foot gap over a steep drop. You can either spend two hours cutting a safe bypass through dense brush, or carefully cross the mudslide using a single anchored rope to save time.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Faced with a damaged trail just after escaping the gorge flood, how do you navigate?

options.label: A
options.title: The Aggressive Cross
options.text: Anchor your rope and cross the slide one by one. You argue that maintaining velocity and beating the dropping temperature overrides the risk of a slip.

options.label: B
options.title: The Deliberate Bypass
options.text: Spend two hours clearing a secure path through the brush. You argue that exposing exhausted assets to an unverified drop is a safety failure.

options.label: C
options.title: The Distributed Scout
options.text: Send two agile members to verify if the mudslide is stable while the others begin digging the bypass. You argue that you should test the primary option before committing the whole team.

options.label: D
options.title: The Absolute Halt
options.text: "Order the team to build an emergency fire and wait until daylight conditions improve or the terrain can be reassessed."

scenarios.title: The Ambiguous Opening
scenarios.narrativeText: It is 4:30 PM. You have cleared the final gorge obstacle. As you climb the last ridge, you spot a semi-concealed opening in the cliffside. It isn't just a cave; you see the faint, geometric lines of cut stone and a rusted iron hinge buried in the mud—a clear sign of human-made infrastructure from a past era. The trailhead is only a mile away. Two members are already moving toward it to investigate, while the others are hesitant, worried that this structure might be unstable, hazardous, or simply an irrelevant distraction from your mission.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Facing an unexpected, man-made opportunity near the finish line, what is your strategic response?

options.label: A
options.title: The Agile Assessment
options.text: You order a "quick look" protocol. You and the lead scout enter for a rapid, five-minute assessment of the structure's nature and stability, while the rest of the team maintains a fixed position at the ridge. You prioritize high-speed information gathering to see if this represents a high-value asset or a dead end.

options.label: B
options.title: The Collaborative Pivot
options.text: You move the entire team to the entrance and authorize a 20-minute group exploration. You argue that the team's collective intelligence is your greatest asset, and any discovery here (historical, structural, or logistical) should be vetted by the whole unit to ensure all perspectives are represented.

options.label: C
options.title: The Mission Purist
options.text: You classify the structure as an "out-of-scope distraction." You mandate immediate continuation to the trailhead, arguing that success is defined by delivering the team to the objective on time, not by chasing undocumented curiosities.

options.label: D
options.title: The Structural Audit
options.text: You treat the find as a potential project of record. You establish a formal 30-minute block to document, photograph, and safely evaluate the exterior and entrance, weighing the potential long-term value of the find against the immediate cost of the delay.

scenarios.title: The Commitment Bottleneck
scenarios.narrativeText: You have officially moved into the investigation phase. The passage has narrowed into a difficult bottleneck. You can see that the corridor continues into a deeper, larger space, but it is obscured—you cannot yet determine what lies beyond or if the passage remains viable for the whole team. Reversing course after committing more people and equipment through this gap will be extremely difficult and time-consuming.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You have passed the initial "is this worth a look?" stage. Now you face the "how deep do we go?" commitment. How do you advance?

options.label: A
options.title: The Lead-from-the-Front
options.text: You commit yourself through the bottleneck first to personally vet the environment, setting a standard for the team to follow. You argue that the leader must absorb the initial exposure to risk to provide the group with the confidence to proceed.

options.label: B
options.title: The Resource-First approach
options.text: You prioritize moving the necessary gear and infrastructure through the gap first, optimizing the environment before moving the personnel. You argue that you should never move people into a high-friction zone until the support systems are fully established.

options.label: C
options.title: The Risk-Mitigation approach
options.text: You pause and conduct a thorough analysis of the bottleneck's stability and the potential exit routes before moving a single person forward. You argue that "commitment" is a function of safety, and you will not move until you have eliminated all avoidable variables.

options.label: D
options.title: The Probe approach
options.text: You keep the team in a secure, static position and send only a minimal, specialized "probe" team forward to confirm the value of the space beyond. You argue that you should never commit the full organization until the return on investment is verified.

scenarios.title: The Internal Discovery
scenarios.narrativeText:
** Your commitment strategy has succeeded; you have reached the deeper chamber. It is not a natural cave, but a forgotten, 18th-century subterranean storage facility. It is filled with rotted wooden crates, oxidized iron tools, and what appears to be a cache of historical military supplies. It is a significant find, but the atmosphere is heavy and the floor is uneven. A faint, low-frequency hum vibrates through the floor—likely a distant underground water source or a structural resonance—and you have no clear sense of how long this facility has been sealed.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You are now inside the "opportunity." How do you allocate your team's limited capacity to maximize this discovery while maintaining operational integrity?

options.label: A
options.title: The Rapid Documentation
options.text: You order an immediate, high-speed documentation phase. Everyone pulls out their mobile devices to photograph, log, and map the items in place. You argue that capturing the data is the priority; physical contact must be minimized to avoid damaging the site or risking injury.

options.label: B
options.title: The Surgical Extraction
options.text: You designate a "primary recovery team" to select the most historically significant artifacts for immediate transport, while the rest of the team monitors the room's structural stability. You argue that the value of the find is only realized through possession and preservation.

options.label: C
options.title: The Structural Survey
options.text: You halt all handling of artifacts to focus on mapping the facility's architecture. You believe the true value lies in understanding the engineering and original purpose of the site, arguing that artifacts are secondary to the historical context of the structure itself.

options.label: D
options.title: The Strategic Exit
options.text: You designate this as a "protected zone." After a quick, baseline visual scan, you order everyone out and seal the entrance as best as possible. You argue that the team is not equipped to curate this site, and full engagement would be a catastrophic drain on your primary mission resources.

scenarios.title: The Prior Claimant
scenarios.narrativeText: As you conclude your mapping of the storage facility, you discover something that stops you cold: a set of maintenance logs and recently replaced equipment. The facility is not a historical relic; it is an active, currently operated site. You are standing in the middle of a competitor's or a prior claimant's active operation. You have not been spotted yet, but your presence is now an unauthorized intrusion into an existing stakeholder's workspace.
scenarios.decisionPoint: The opportunity you identified is already under active management by an unknown party. How do you respond?

options.label: A
options.title: The Transparent Engagement
options.text: You remain in place and wait for the operators to arrive, intending to initiate a formal introduction. You argue that the most professional approach to a conflict of interest is open communication and seeking a potential partnership or clear resolution.

options.label: B
options.title: The Quiet Disengagement
options.text: You immediately stop all documentation, erase any trace of your presence, and vacate the site via the route you entered. You argue that once a "prior claimant" is identified, the value of the opportunity is negated by the risk of conflict, and the only logical move is to withdraw.

options.label: C
options.title: The Strategic Pivot
options.text: You exit the facility but mark the perimeter, intending to research who the claimant is before taking further action. You argue that you should never engage or abandon an opportunity until you understand the scale and nature of the opposition.

options.label: D
options.title: The Measured Observation
options.text: You position the team in a discreet location to observe the site for a limited window to identify the operators and their activities before deciding on a course of action. You argue that intelligence is the most valuable asset in any competitive environment, and you cannot make a rational decision without data.

scenarios.title: The Incumbent's Terms
scenarios.narrativeText:
** You opted to observe the facility from a discreet position. You have confirmed that the "prior claimant" is a small, professional team utilizing the site for specialized logistics. As you prepare to finalize your departure, they spot you. They do not initiate hostilities, but their security lead approaches your position, clearly expecting an explanation for your presence. They are well-equipped, organized, and hold the clear advantage of being on "home turf."
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You are now in a face-to-face negotiation with an incumbent operator. How do you manage this high-stakes interaction?

options.label: A
options.title: The Full Transparency Approach
options.text: You immediately disclose your purpose, your discovery of the site, and your plans to leave. You argue that honesty is the only way to establish credibility and minimize the risk of being viewed as a threat or a competitor.

options.label: B
options.title: The Controlled De
options.text: escalation):** You provide a limited, curated explanation—framing your presence as a navigational error—and request an immediate, mutually agreeable path to exit. You argue that providing just enough truth to be plausible while minimizing shared information is the safest way to disengage.

options.label: C
options.title: The Assertive Reciprocity
options.text: You treat the encounter as a professional meeting between peers. You acknowledge their operations without asking questions, establish your own credentials, and propose a professional exchange of information or a "non-interference" pact. You argue that appearing as a subordinate or a trespasser is a failure of leadership.

options.label: D
options.title: The Strategic Ambiguity
options.text: You maintain a polite but deliberately vague posture, declining to explain your presence in detail while emphasizing your intent to vacate the area. You argue that revealing your identity, your objectives, or your team's capacity is an unnecessary compromise of your future competitive advantage.

scenarios.title: The Intellectual Property Ultimatum
scenarios.narrativeText: The incumbent security lead clarifies the terms: they are engaged in proprietary geological mining research. They view your presence—and your digital records—as a breach of their trade secrets. They offer you a choice: exit via their high-speed logistical route, provided you surrender your digital storage media (containing your site maps, structural photos, and survey data). Or, exit via the arduous, miles-long original ridge trail, keeping your data intact but leaving your team exposed to exhaustion and the rapidly fading daylight.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You must weigh the value of your proprietary intelligence against the immediate operational safety of your team. What is your call?

options.label: A
options.title: The Strategic Retention
options.text: You refuse to surrender the data and choose the arduous route. You argue that the research data you've collected is an invaluable strategic asset, and no competitor has the right to demand the surrender of your proprietary findings.

options.label: B
options.title: The Operational Prioritization
options.text: You surrender the media and take the high-speed route. You argue that the primary mission is the safe, timely extraction of your team; the research data is secondary to the personnel's well-being.

options.label: C
options.title: The Professional Compromise
options.text: You offer to present your data to them for immediate "sanitization"—deleting only the specific geological coordinates—while retaining the rest of your findings. You argue that professional engagement relies on finding a middle path that addresses their security concerns without sacrificing your mission results.

options.label: D
options.title: The Long-Term Alignment
options.text: You surrender the media in its entirety, but use the extraction time to build rapport with the researchers, viewing the "loss" of data as a down payment on a potential future partnership in this territory. You argue that long-term relationships are worth more than a single set of survey data.

scenarios.title: The Integrity of the Return
scenarios.narrativeText: You have successfully departed the mining research site. Whether you walked the long path or took the logistical exit, you are now back on safe, neutral ground as night fully falls. Your team is physically exhausted. As you debrief, the weight of the last few hours hits: if you surrendered the data, your team is safe but your primary objective—the research and documentation—is essentially nullified. If you kept the data, you have a valuable, hard-won asset, but the team is shattered, morale is low, and your relationship with the local operators is permanently adversarial.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Looking back at the cost of the exit, how do you frame this experience to the team to ensure long-term unit cohesion and mission success?

options.label: A
options.title: The Mission-Centric Briefing
options.text: You validate the sacrifice as necessary for the project. You focus entirely on the data gathered (or the lessons learned), arguing that objective accomplishment is the only metric that matters to the organization.

options.label: B
options.title: The Human-Centric Briefing
options.text: You emphasize the team's resilience and your decision to prioritize their safety above all else. You argue that the team is the only truly irreplaceable asset, and no objective justifies their destruction or unnecessary endangerment.

options.label: C
options.title: The Accountability Briefing
options.text: You take full responsibility for the tension between the goal and the risk, openly discussing why the encounter went the way it did. You argue that transparency builds trust, and that acknowledging the difficulty of the call is the best way to prevent resentment.

options.label: D
options.title: The Future-Oriented Briefing
options.text: You frame the encounter as a "successful intelligence gathering mission" regardless of the outcome, shifting the focus to what you learned about the competitor's operations. You argue that framing every challenge as an intelligence win keeps the team focused on the big picture rather than local setbacks.

scenarios.title: The Competitive Lever
scenarios.narrativeText: You have recovered from the encounter and are back in a stable operational environment. You have synthesized your findings: the other team is a well-funded venture operating in a highly contested and poorly understood regulatory environment. You now possess proprietary intelligence regarding their methodology and their presence in the territory. This information gives you significant leverage, but acting on it will inevitably draw you into a long-term competitive struggle.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You now have leverage over a competitor. How do you integrate this knowledge into your long-term strategy?

options.label: A
options.title: The Institutional Escalation
options.text: You leverage your findings to lobby for formal regulatory clarity in the region, effectively changing the rules of the game to favor your operating model over theirs. You argue that shaping the environment to your advantage is the most effective way to secure a permanent lead.

options.label: B
options.title: The Partnership Strategy
options.text: You approach the competitor with your findings as a basis for a collaborative venture, arguing that the "contested" nature of the region makes cooperation more profitable than conflict. You argue that combining your intelligence with their infrastructure creates a monopoly position.

options.label: C
options.title: The Strategic Repositioning
options.text: You keep the information private and use it to preemptively occupy adjacent, high-value sectors before the competitor realizes their full potential. You argue that outmaneuvering the competition through superior positioning is better than engaging them in a direct, resource-draining contest.

options.label: D
options.title: The Strategic Disengagement
options.text: You archive the intelligence for future reference but decide to pivot your organization's efforts toward an entirely different territory. You argue that the complexity and potential for conflict in this region represent an unacceptable drain on your organization's agility and focus.

scenarios.title: The Transition to the Basin
scenarios.narrativeText: You've successfully cleared the quarry perimeter and are trekking toward the coastal basin. The topography changes from dense, industrial-scarred hills to a wide, winding river delta. It is late afternoon, and the light is playing tricks on the horizon. Ahead, you spot a lone figure in a small, flat-bottomed boat, navigating the shallows with a long pole and a sophisticated, handheld sonar unit. They aren't a researcher or a competitor—they seem to be a local, but they are clearly looking for something specific under the riverbed.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You have a clear line of sight, but the individual has not yet noticed your team on the bank. They are working in a section of the river that, according to your preliminary maps, shouldn't have any commercial value. How do you approach this contact?

options.label: A
options.title: The Overt Greeting
options.text: You wave and signal to get their attention, walking down to the water's edge to ask about the currents and the area's history. You argue that locals are the most valuable source of "ground truth" and that showing open respect is the best way to earn their cooperation.

options.label: B
options.title: The Low-Profile Observation
options.text: You stay hidden in the brush and observe their patterns. You argue that watching their technique—and seeing what they are actually looking for—tells you more about the region's hidden potential than a conversation ever could.

options.label: C
options.title: The Tactical Bypass
options.text: You maintain your path, keeping your distance, and ignore them entirely. You argue that any interaction with locals carries unnecessary risk; your mission focus is your priority, and curiosity is a potential distraction.

options.label: D
options.title: The Strategic Probe
options.text: You send one team member to intercept them at a future point downstream to strike up a casual conversation and compare the information they provide with your team's observations. You argue that indirect inquiry yields the most honest and balanced intelligence.
