scenarios.title: The General Store Stop
scenarios.narrativeText: You've finally cleared the mud and grit of the quarry, and the sun is finally breaking through the clouds. You're damp, your pack is heavy, and your boots are soaked through. You stumble upon a rustic general store right by the riverbank. It smells like fresh coffee and pine. Inside, the owner sees your state and points to a rack of gear and a stack of life vests. "Look," they say, "for ten bucks a person, you can rent a canoe right here. It'll take you the rest of the way to the pickup point at the park entrance. It's a lot smoother than hiking the mud, and if you're quiet, you'll see deer, turtles in the bogs, and maybe even a moose near the narrows. Just watch the current if you aren't a strong swimmer."
scenarios.decisionPoint: You're standing in the store, looking at your soggy gear and the calm, winding river outside. The canoes are ready, and the river is calling. How do you prepare to launch?

options.label: A
options.title: The "Wildlife Expedition"
options.text: You prioritize camera gear and binoculars. You're here to see the animals, so you organize the boats to be slow, quiet, and perfect for spotting moose in the brush.

options.label: B
options.title: The "River Navigators"
options.text:
You prioritize 
speed and efficiency. You check the current maps and pair up your strongest paddlers to ensure you can handle the bogs and the narrow channels without getting stuck.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Casual Drifters"
options.text: You grab some extra snacks and drinks from the store and plan to tie the boats together for a relaxing, social drift down to the pickup point. You're here to enjoy the ride, not race it.

options.label: D
options.title: The "Safety-First Crew"
options.text: You check every life vest twice and put your strongest swimmer in the lead boat to scout for hazards. You want to make sure everyone—especially the less experienced—is confident before you push off.

scenarios.title: The First Bend
scenarios.narrativeText:
** You've been on the water for about an hour. The river is peaceful, the sun is warm, and you're just starting to get the rhythm of the paddles. Suddenly, you come around a gentle bend and find your path partially blocked. A local fisherman in a weathered aluminum boat is anchored right in the middle of the narrowest part of the channel, casting lines toward the reeds. He's completely unbothered, humming to himself, and doesn't seem to notice your group approaching. The channel is just wide enough for you to squeeze by if you're careful, but one wrong move could tip a canoe or snag a line.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You have to navigate past this unexpected "obstacle" without ruining his morning—or getting your gear soaked. How do you handle it?

options.label: A
options.title: The Polite Request
options.text: You call out a friendly, "Morning, sir! Mind if we slip by?" You're banking on the fact that a little transparency goes a long way and might even lead to a tip about where the best fishing (or wildlife) is.

options.label: B
options.title: The Silent Glide
options.text: You instruct the group to stop paddling and just drift silently past him, hugging the opposite bank. You want to avoid interrupting his peace, respecting the "unspoken code" of the river.

options.label: C
options.title: The Curious Conversation
options.text: You slow down and steer closer to strike up a chat. You're genuinely curious about what he's catching, and you figure he's the best person to ask about local conditions, upcoming hazards, or where the moose have been hiding lately ,yet  chatting to him could cost you time.

options.label: D
options.title: The Tactical Maneuver
options.text: You scan the water for his lines, signal the rest of your canoes to stay in a tight line, and navigate through the narrow gap with precision. You treat it like a minor portage challenge—get through it clean, stay focused, and keep moving.

scenarios.title: The Riverbank Legend
scenarios.narrativeText:
** After you drift past the fisherman, he calls out a friendly warning: "You folks headed toward the lower bogs? Keep your eyes peeled. The fog gets thick down there, and there's a lot of folks who've come back from the narrows swearing they've seen things that don't belong in these woods." He chuckles, clearly enjoying the myth-making, but his eyes are serious. As you continue downstream, the atmosphere shifts. The trees grow denser, the light dims, and you hear a strange, rhythmic snapping sound—like heavy branches breaking—coming from the brush just ahead of you on the bank.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** Your team is alert, the silence of the woods is suddenly heavy, and that "Bigfoot" legend the fisherman alluded to feels a lot less funny than it did ten minutes ago. How do you react to the unexpected noise?

options.label: A
options.title: The "Call Out"
options.text: You project your voice clearly: "Hello? Is someone there?" You're choosing to humanize the situation immediately, assuming it's another camper or a park ranger, and you want to dispel any tension before it builds.

options.label: B
options.title: The "Silent Pause"
options.text: You raise your paddle to signal the rest of the group to stop. You drift silently, listening to see if the sound repeats or if it moves. You're gathering information before you decide whether to proceed or pivot.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Playful Skeptic"
options.text: You laugh it off, maybe even making a loud, exaggerated Bigfoot call to break the tension. You're betting that it's just a deer or a bear and you want to keep morale high by refusing to let the spooky atmosphere affect the team.

options.label: D
options.title: The "Vigilant Guard"
options.text: You steer the canoes toward the center of the river, away from the dense bank, keeping your eyes locked on the treeline. You're prepared for a wild animal, and you want to maintain a "safety buffer" between your team and the unknown source of the noise.

scenarios.title: The "Big" Reveal
scenarios.narrativeText:
** You hold your breath as the branches part. Whatever was making that noise is definitely large—you can see the brush shaking violently just ten feet from the water. Suddenly, a massive, shaggy shape bursts out from behind a willow tree and thunders into the shallow water with a splash that nearly swamps your canoe. It's not a cryptid or a monster; it's a bull moose, startled by your drift, shaking water from its coat like a wet dog. It stares at you for a heartbeat—huge, imposing, and completely wild—before turning and wading gracefully into the deep reeds of the bog.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** The adrenaline is still pumping, and the team is buzzing with excitement. This is the highlight of the trip so far, but you're now running slightly behind schedule, and the bog you're approaching is known for being tricky to navigate. How do you capitalize on this moment?

options.label: A
options.title: The "Group Debrief"
options.text: You pull the canoes into a small eddy and take a ten-minute break to let everyone catch their breath and share the story. You want to cement the memory as a shared team victory before refocusing on the navigation.

options.label: B
options.title: The "Photographic Sprint"
options.text: You quickly grab the cameras and scramble to get a few shots of the moose in the distance. You're balancing the thrill of the encounter with the need to keep moving toward the pickup point.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Navigator's Push"
options.text: You don't stop. You acknowledge the encounter with a cheer, but you keep the paddles moving hard. You're worried that the moose was spooked by *something*—or someone—else nearby, and you want to put distance between your team and the spot.

options.label: D
options.title: The "Nature Study"
options.text: You move the canoes slowly toward where the moose entered the reeds, looking for tracks or signs. You're curious about the habitat and want to use this as an impromptu learning moment for the team to better understand the river's ecosystem.

scenarios.title: The Bog Labyrinth
scenarios.narrativeText:
** The encounter with the bull moose was exhilarating, but it led you into the heart of the "lower bogs." The river has fragmented into a maze of narrow, stagnant channels choked with lily pads and dense, submerged vegetation. The water is glassy and still. The map you have is vague, and the current has virtually vanished. You realize the "main channel" is no longer obvious, and the team is starting to drift in different directions. The sun is beginning to drop, casting long, confusing shadows through the reeds.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You need to find the exit path to the main river before nightfall. How do you re-establish control and route your team?

options.label: A
options.title: The Scout Ahead
options.text: You send the fastest boat ahead to "dead-end check" the different channels while the others hold back. You argue that splitting the labor to find the path is faster than waiting for everyone to agree on a direction.

options.label: B
options.title: The "Back to Basics" Consensus
options.text: You call for a stop, gather the boats, and have everyone compare their personal observations—what looked like moving water, where the birds were flying, and the angle of the sun. You argue that collective intelligence is the safest way to navigate an unmapped area.

options.label: C
options.title: The Systematic Sweep
options.text: You instruct the group to form a line abreast, sweeping through the widest gap together. You're sacrificing speed for safety, ensuring that if one boat hits a dead end or a hidden hazard, the whole group is close enough to pivot immediately.

options.label: D
options.title: The Environmental Reader
options.text: You steer your canoe to the edge of the reeds to look for "flow signs"—bent grass, disturbed silt, or the direction insects are congregating—to identify the path of least resistance. You're betting that the river's natural behavior will point the way out better than a map.

scenarios.title: The Sunset Squeeze
scenarios.narrativeText:
** The light is failing fast, turning the bog into a silhouette of tall reeds and dark water. Just as the team is starting to feel the heat of the situation, you spot a break in the vegetation. It leads to a narrow, high-walled passage that wasn't on your map. It's tight—barely enough room for a single canoe—but you can feel a subtle change in the water pressure; it's finally flowing again. However, the passage is lined with jagged, weathered rocks that look like they could easily tear the hull of your rental canoes if you bump them in the gloom.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You have to commit to this passage before you lose the remaining twilight, but it's a high-risk, high-reward bottleneck. What is your strategy?

options.label: A
options.title: The Controlled Tether
options.text: You stop and tie all the canoes together into a single, long "train." You put the most experienced paddler in the front and the best rudder in the back. It's slower, but you ensure the entire group stays aligned and protected from the rocks.

options.label: B
options.title: The Individual Push
options.text: You instruct everyone to take the passage one at a time, spacing them out by thirty seconds. You argue that the risk of a "pile-up" in the dark is higher than the risk of an individual hull breach, and you want each boat to have 100% control of their own path.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Bump and Drag"
options.text: You decide to get out of the canoes and wade through the shallow, muddy edges of the passage, guiding the boats by hand. It's physically exhausting and you'll be covered in mud, but it guarantees zero hull damage and keeps the team together in the dark.

options.label: D
options.title: The Aggressive Sprint
options.text: You take the lead, paddling hard to hit the passage with enough momentum to keep the canoe straight, signaling the others to follow your exact wake. You argue that speed and precision are the only ways to navigate tight, rocky water without drifting into the hazards.

scenarios.title: The Hidden Campfire
scenarios.narrativeText:
** You navigate the narrow passage safely, the canoes scraping only slightly against the rock. As you emerge, the narrow walls widen suddenly into a hidden, circular cove sheltered by towering pines. It's completely dark now, but your eyes adjust to see the flicker of a warm, inviting campfire on the shore. It's not the pickup point—you're still a few miles from that—but it's an established, unofficial campsite. A small group of people is sitting there, guitars in hand, with the smell of roasting sausages drifting across the water. They look like locals who know exactly where they are.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You're exhausted, hungry, and the pickup point is still a trek through the dark. You have two choices: push through the final miles or land and ask to share their fire. How do you approach this?

options.label: A
options.title: The "Invite
options.text: Only" Approach):** You drift near the shore and call out a friendly greeting, asking if they have room for a group of tired paddlers to share the fire for an hour. You figure the social connection is worth the delay in reaching your final destination.

options.label: B
options.title: The "Shadow Land"
options.text: You pull your canoes into a dark spot fifty yards down the bank, keeping your light disciplined. You set up your own camp quietly near theirs—close enough to benefit from their light and sense of safety, but far enough to maintain your team's privacy and independence.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Silent Transit"
options.text: You don't make a sound. You signal the team to keep their paddles in the water and glide past the cove into the darkness of the river. You argue that your team's objective is the pickup point, and unpredictable social encounters late at night are a variable you don't need.

options.label: D
options.title: The "Supply Trade"
options.text: You pull up and offer a few snacks, coffee, or spare supplies in exchange for a warm spot to dry out and their take on the final stretch of the river. You're looking to make a simple, natural exchange that gets you to the finish line informed and refreshed.

scenarios.title: The Final Push
scenarios.narrativeText:
** After your interaction at the campfire, you're back on the water. The river has widened significantly, and the rhythmic sound of your paddles is the only thing cutting through the night. Ahead, you see a faint, artificial glow—the lights of the main park entrance and the rental pickup point. You're close, but the water here is deep and the current is stronger than it looks. You notice a marked channel that takes a long, slow curve around a sandbar, and an "unofficial" shortcut that cuts straight through a cluster of pilings from an old, collapsed dock.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You are minutes away from the end of the journey. Do you play it safe, or do you take the risk to finish the trip faster?

options.label: A
options.title: The "Official Route"
options.text: You stick to the marked channel. It adds time to your trip, but you've come this far without losing a canoe; you aren't going to risk a puncture on old dock pilings just to save ten minutes.

options.label: B
options.title: The "Calculated Shortcut"
options.text: You aim for the gap in the pilings. You trust your night vision and your team's ability to navigate the debris. You argue that if you've handled bogs, moose, and rocky passages, you can handle a little timber in the water.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Night
options.text: Drift Finish"):** You stop paddling entirely and let the river carry you toward the lights. You want to savor the last few minutes of the trip, letting the current take you home without rushing the end.

options.label: D
options.title: The "Team Coordination"
options.text: You have the lead boat scout the pilings with a high-lumen flashlight while the rest of the group holds position. You'll only take the shortcut if the scout confirms it's clear, balancing the desire for speed with the reality of the hazards.

scenarios.title: Hours Drift
scenarios.narrativeText:
** You've reached the park's main pickup point, but it's crowded, loud, and feels more like a parking lot than a wilderness camp. You're beat, it's pitch black, and the prospect of setting up a tent under a harsh streetlamp is killing your mood. However, the canoe rental contract requires you to drop the boats at this specific landing. You realize that if you push just a mile further downstream, you'll be outside the park's main jurisdiction and into a quiet, secluded stretch of woods where you can have a real campfire. But, you'd be breaking the "official" return protocol, and you'd have to hike back or portage the gear in the morning.
**
scenarios.decisionPoint: ** You're standing on the bank with the canoes. The park attendant is busy with another group, and the moon is just bright enough to navigate the next bend. How do you play this?

options.label: A
options.title: The "Rule Follower"
options.text: You unload and turn in the canoes as instructed. You prioritize the contract and the "official" end of the trip, even if it means sacrificing a better camping experience.

options.label: B
options.title: The "Unauthorized Extension"
options.text: You decide to keep the canoes for the night, pushing downstream to the quiet woods. You're willing to deal with the minor penalty fees or awkward explanations in the morning because the quality of the camp matters more than the bureaucracy.

options.label: C
options.title: The "Night Hike"
options.text: You drop the canoes off, but leave the gear behind and trek into the dark woods on foot to find a better spot, planning to walk back to the pickup point at sunrise to deal with the logistics.

options.label: D
options.title: The "Negotiator"
options.text: You walk up to the attendant, explain that you're looking for a better spot, and ask if there's a "grace period" or a spot they recommend nearby that isn't the main landing. You're trying to find a legal way to get your ideal campsite.

scenarios.title: The Hunting Camp
scenarios.narrativeText:
You've pushed downstream to a secluded bend and found a derelict hunting camp. It consists of three small, weathered cabins, each in a different state of decay. On the threshold of the center cabin, there is a hand-carved inscription beginning with the letter "H," but it is oddly, almost jaggedly, carved—as if the person struggled with the wood or was in a hurry. The cabins themselves are distinct:
The Collapsed Cabin: A structure with a caved-in roof, but the fieldstone foundation looks remarkably sturdy.
The Inscribed Cabin: The center one with the odd "H" carving, which feels oddly preserved compared to the others.
The Sealed Cabin: A small, windowless hut with a heavy, iron-bound door that looks like it hasn't been opened in decades.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You have limited time and daylight. Where do you focus your attention to learn more about this site?

options.label: A
options.title: The Architectural Analyst
options.text: You inspect the foundation of the Collapsed Cabin. You're interested in how this place was built and why it failed, believing the structural history—and why the roof collapsed while the foundation held—tells you more about the site than a carving could.

options.label: B
options.title: The Historian
options.text: You focus on the Inscribed Cabin. You find yourself looking at that jagged "H," wondering what prompted someone to carve it with such urgency, and what kind of person felt the need to leave that mark behind.

options.label: C
options.title: The Structural Investigator
options.text: You approach the Sealed Cabin. You are curious why this was the only building intentionally fortified or sealed, and you want to understand the logic behind why it was treated differently than the other two.

options.label: D
options.title: The Site Planner
options.text: You walk the perimeter of the entire camp, ignoring the doors for now. You're looking for the "why"—the relationship between the structures, how the camp was oriented toward the river, and how the three buildings once functioned as a single unit.

scenarios.title: The Gathering Storm
scenarios.narrativeText:
The air turns heavy and metallic—the kind of humidity that precedes a massive summer thunderstorm. The wind suddenly shifts. Rain begins hammering the clearing, turning the dry pine needles into a slick mess. You have to get the team under cover, or at least stabilize your camp. You're standing in the clearing with the three structures:
The Collapsed Cabin: The roof is gone, but the fieldstone fireplace is massive and intact. You can rig a large, heavy-duty tarp over the remaining walls to create a dry, semi-open-air hearth that will keep the team warm and the gear accessible.
The Inscribed Cabin: It is completely enclosed, dry, and smells of aged pine. It appears almost frozen in time, with a small wooden table, a rusted stove, and a neatly stacked pile of split logs remaining. It offers immediate, total shelter, but the space is cramped.
The Sealed Cabin: The heavy, iron-bound door appears structurally sound, but no one knows why it was originally sealed. Forcing the door ensures total protection from the elements, but it requires destruction of property and risks exposing the team to unknown structural hazards, wildlife, or hazardous conditions inside.
scenarios.decisionPoint: The storm is hitting with full force. You have mere seconds to decide where to move the team and gear.

options.label: A
options.title: The Hearth Strategy
options.text: You commit to the Collapsed Cabin. You're prioritizing the utility of the fireplace and the ability to modify the environment (the tarp) to suit your needs. You prefer to adapt what is already there rather than gamble on the unknown.

options.label: B
options.title: The Preservation Strategy
options.text: You choose the Inscribed Cabin. You want the total, dry enclosure of a standing structure, and you're willing to adapt to the cramped, "frozen-in-time" atmosphere to ensure everyone is out of the wind and rain immediately.

options.label: C
options.title: The Breach Strategy
options.text: You prioritize total security from the elements. You choose the Sealed Cabin, deciding that the uncertainty of what is inside is a risk worth taking to ensure your team is shielded in a structurally sound, fully enclosed building.

options.label: D
options.title: The Perimeter Strategy
options.text: You refuse to enter the structures. You trust your own tents and gear more than the integrity of these aging buildings. You'll anchor down in the brush, maintaining your independence and keeping your team entirely self-sufficient, even if it means getting wet while you set up.

scenarios.title: The Night Watch
scenarios.narrativeText:
You've successfully established your base. The storm is raging outside, drumming against the wood and canvas, creating a rhythmic, isolating roar that makes the outside world feel miles away. Inside your chosen shelter—the hearth, the inscribed room, the sealed room, or your own tents—the adrenaline of the storm is beginning to wane, and the reality of your surroundings is setting in. You have a few hours before dawn, and while the team is settling down, you have the watch.
The silence inside is different from the chaos outside. You notice subtle details you missed in the rush: a loose floorboard, a draft coming from an impossible angle, or a piece of charcoal on the ground that looks like it was recently dropped.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You are sitting in the dark, listening to the storm. How do you spend the time while the others sleep?

options.label: A
options.title: The Maintenance Loop
options.text: You focus entirely on the gear. You check the seals on the equipment, dry out damp clothes by the fire (or stove), and organize your kit for a rapid departure at sunrise. You believe the best way to handle the mystery of the night is to ensure the team is ready for any contingency.

options.label: B
options.title: The Environmental Audit
options.text: You use your light to carefully trace the origin of that draft or look for the source of the loose floorboard. You aren't looking for trouble, but you have a compulsive need to understand the "physics" of your temporary home—how it breathes, how it was built, and where it leaks.

options.label: C
options.title: The Quiet Archive
options.text: You sit still and observe. You're letting the house "talk." You want to see if the building settles in a particular way, if the shadows shift, or if you can detect the faint sounds of the woods outside that aren't drowned out by the rain. You're looking for patterns in the environment.

options.label: D
options.title: The Security Scan
options.text: You move to the entrance of your shelter to monitor the periphery. You're watching the storm, but your primary concern is the clearing itself. You want to see if anything—or anyone—else is moving out there in the dark, treating your shelter as a position to be defended rather than just a place to rest.

scenarios.title: The Morning Discovery
scenarios.narrativeText:
You wake up as the light begins to filter through the cracks in the walls. In the soft, low-angle morning sun, you notice dozens of carvings you completely missed in the dark. They are everywhere—on the interior door frames, the window sills, and the exposed support beams. As you walk between the three cabins, the range of messages becomes clear:
The Memorials: Some are simple and poignant—dates, names, and tributes like "For my father, 1952" or "In memory of the long winters."
The Mundane/Territorial: Others are purely practical or assertive: "No trespassing," lists of gear inventories, or tally marks documenting years of hunting seasons.
The Ambiguous/Ritualistic: Scattered among these are strange, complex geometric symbols and recurring patterns that don't look like English—not necessarily "evil," but clearly holding a weight or meaning to the people who carved them.
The Youthful/Impulsive: There are also the undeniable marks of boredom—crude drawings, names of local teenagers, and the kind of "I was here" vandalism that happens anywhere there's a quiet place to hide.
scenarios.decisionPoint: You have a clear picture of the layer upon layer of human history here. Before you leave, what do you focus on?

options.label: A
options.title: The Archivist
options.text: You spend extra time photographing and sketching the most significant markings. You feel a responsibility to preserve the human story before weather and decay erase it.

options.label: B
options.title: The Custodian
options.text: You don't add your own mark, and you carefully leave the cabins exactly as you found them. You erase signs of your stay, believing the site should remain undisturbed.

options.label: C
options.title: The Contributor
options.text: You carve a small, respectful mark of your own—a date or initials—adding your presence to the long history of people who have passed through the camp.

options.label: D
options.title: The Evaluator
options.text: Rather than focusing on individual carvings, you study what they collectively reveal about the people who occupied the camp across different generations.

scenarios.title: The Pattern Reveal
scenarios.narrativeText:
The storm has passed. As the sun rises in the east, the light hitting the clearing exposes a striking detail. By aligning the three cabins, you realize the layout is far from random. The "Collapsed Cabin," the "Inscribed Cabin," and the "Sealed Cabin" are all oriented toward distinct landmarks on the far side of the river: a lightning-scarred pine, a jagged rock formation, and a narrow, hidden inlet. The alignment appears intentional. Whatever these cabins were built for, their placement was unlikely to be accidental.
You have one last opportunity to examine the interiors with this new understanding of their spatial relationship.
scenarios.decisionPoint: How do you synthesize the evidence to form your theory of the site?

options.label: A
options.title: The Functional Analysis
options.text: You return to the Collapsed Cabin. You believe that if this site had a practical purpose, the evidence will be found in the material remains: the tools, wear patterns, construction techniques, and discarded materials. You are looking for the "how"—the physical work that once occurred here.

options.label: B
options.title: The Documentary Analysis
options.text: You revisit the Inscribed Cabin. You suspect the carvings, dates, and markings are more than decoration; they are the record-keeping system for the camp. You are searching for a log, a map, or a chronology that explains the "who" and the "when" of this operation.

options.label: C
options.title: The Protective Analysis
options.text: You examine the Sealed Cabin. The immense effort required to isolate and reinforce this building suggests it served a unique, critical function. You are interested in the "why"—why this specific structure required greater security than the rest of the camp.

options.label: D
options.title: The Holistic Synthesis
options.text:
You don't pick one. You stand in the exact center of the clearing, where the lines of sight between the cabins and the landmarks intersect. You are attempting to visualize the site as a single, integrated instrument, trying to understand how the three buildings functioned in tandem to monitor or manage the landscape across the river.
Whether it was a survey station, a trapping operation, an early forestry outpost, or something else entirely, one conclusion is unavoidable: every feature of the camp appears to have served a purpose.

scenarios.title: The Final Evidence
scenarios.narrativeText: Before leaving the clearing, you decide to take one last walk through the camp. With your new understanding of the cabins' alignment, small details suddenly begin to fit together. You notice axe marks on certain trees, worn footpaths that don't lead to the river, and subtle differences in the construction of each building. None of these clues answers the mystery outright, but together they point toward a larger purpose. Your team is packed and waiting. You have time to pursue only one final line of inquiry before you leave the site behind.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Where do you focus your final effort?

options.label: A
options.title: The Material Trail
options.text: You follow the old work paths leading away from the camp, looking for evidence of what resources the occupants were harvesting or transporting.

options.label: B
options.title: The Human Trail
options.text: You continue studying the inscriptions, initials, dates, and carved messages, hoping the people themselves left the clearest explanation of the camp's purpose.

options.label: C
options.title: The Defensive Trail
options.text: You inspect the perimeter, searching for old fence lines, lookout positions, caches, or other signs that the camp was designed to protect or control something.

options.label: D
options.title: The Environmental Trail
options.text: You climb to a nearby overlook and study how the cabins relate to the river, surrounding terrain, and distant landmarks, searching for a broader pattern that can only be seen from outside the camp.

scenarios.title: The Farmer's Field
scenarios.narrativeText:
The morning dew still clings to the grass as you and your team finally leave the hunting camp behind. The cabins disappear into the trees behind you. Their purpose remains uncertain, and your notebooks are filled with competing theories rather than definitive answers.
As you emerge from the woods into an open hayfield, you hear the low rumble of an old tractor. An elderly farmer notices your group stepping out of the tree line. He slows to a stop, shuts off the engine, and climbs down. For a few moments, neither of you moves. He is studying your group just as carefully as you're studying him.
Eventually, he starts walking toward you.
scenarios.decisionPoint: How do you handle the first unexpected person you've encountered since leaving the cabins?

options.label: A
options.title: The Open Greeting
options.text: You walk toward him first, introduce yourself, and explain that your group was exploring the old cabins. You believe openness is the fastest way to build trust and learn from local knowledge.

options.label: B
options.title: The Cautious Wait
options.text: You stay where you are and allow the farmer to make the first move. You don't hide, but you prefer to let him establish the tone of the conversation before revealing why you're there.

options.label: C
options.title: The Quiet Observation
options.text: Your first instinct is to move back toward the tree line and quietly observe him from a distance. After realizing he's simply curious rather than threatening, you step forward and begin the conversation.

options.label: D
options.title: The Practical Approach
options.text: Rather than discussing the cabins immediately, you greet him politely and begin with practical questions about the roads, local history, and the quickest route back to the trailhead, letting the conversation naturally develop from there.

scenarios.title: The Farmer's Story
scenarios.narrativeText:
The farmer finally reaches your group, glancing between your muddy boots and the notebooks sticking out of your packs.
He smiles knowingly.
"You boys were up at those cabins, weren't you?"
After listening to your story, he nods.
"Those buildings have been here longer than anybody around here can remember. My grandfather always said they were built over the remains of old longhouses. The carvings? Some of those were left by relatives who used the camp generations ago. Others came from hunters passing through. Over the years hikers, campers, and curious folks all left their own marks. That's why none of it seems to fit together. You're looking at a couple hundred years of different people using the same place for different reasons."
He pauses before adding,
"Most folks go up there looking for one answer. There probably isn't one."
scenarios.decisionPoint: How do you respond to this new perspective?

options.label: A
options.title: The Integrator
options.text: You accept that the site evolved over generations. Rather than searching for a single explanation, you begin seeing it as layers of history built upon one another.

options.label: B
options.title: The Verifier
options.text: You appreciate the farmer's account, but you want to compare it with historical records, archaeological evidence, and old maps before changing your conclusions.

options.label: C
options.title: The Skeptic
options.text: You thank him for the story but remain unconvinced. Local traditions are valuable, yet you believe physical evidence should outweigh oral history.

options.label: D
options.title: The Inquirer
options.text: His explanation raises even more questions. You continue asking about families, land ownership, old roads, and local traditions, hoping to build a richer understanding of the area's history.

scenarios.title: The Way Home
scenarios.narrativeText:
Your conversation with the farmer comes to an end. Looking toward the horizon, you realize just how far you've wandered from where you parked several days ago. The trail back will take hours, and everyone is feeling the weight of the expedition. The farmer notices you glancing down the old dirt road.
He tips his hat and says,
"Well... if you're headed back toward the state park, I've got to haul feed into town. I could throw your packs in the truck and save you boys a long walk."
You still have a little cash left from the trip, enough to offer him something for the trouble if you choose.
scenarios.decisionPoint: How do you get back to your vehicle?

options.label: A
options.title: The Finish on Foot
options.text: You thank the farmer but decline the ride. You committed to the journey on foot, and you intend to finish it the same way.

options.label: B
options.title: The Fair Exchange
options.text: You offer the farmer some of your remaining cash for the ride. You view it as a fair exchange—he saves you time, and you're happy to compensate him for his help.

options.label: C
options.title: The Grateful Acceptance
options.text: You gladly accept the ride if he's already headed that way, thanking him for the kindness but not insisting on payment unless he asks. Sometimes accepting generosity is part of traveling.

options.label: D
options.title: The Practical Compromise
options.text: You ask if he'd be willing to haul the heavy packs while your group hikes the remainder of the distance. That way everyone finishes the journey on foot but without the burden of carrying full loads.

scenarios.title: The Trailhead
scenarios.narrativeText:
The familiar outline of your vehicle finally comes into view. After days in the wilderness, it almost feels out of place sitting quietly in the parking lot. Mud covers your boots, your packs are worn, and your body reminds you of every mile you've walked and paddled.
You unload your gear, toss your packs into the back, and pause before climbing into the driver's seat. The expedition is officially over. Once you turn the key, life will begin moving at its normal pace again.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Before leaving the trailhead, what do you do?

options.label: A
options.title: The Final Check
options.text: You perform one last inspection of your gear and vehicle, making sure nothing was left behind and everything is secured before departing. A successful expedition ends with discipline.

options.label: B
options.title: The Photo Review
options.text: Before driving away, you scroll through the photographs on your camera or phone, reliving the expedition one image at a time while the memories are still fresh.

options.label: C
options.title: The Quiet Moment
options.text: You sit silently for a few minutes, looking back toward the forest without speaking. You simply allow yourself to appreciate the experience before returning to everyday life.

options.label: D
options.title: The Next Adventure
options.text: Before even starting the engine, you begin discussing where the group should go next. The expedition has only increased your desire to explore somewhere new.

scenarios.title: Returning to Routine
scenarios.narrativeText:
Several hours later, you arrive home. The expedition has officially ended. Your equipment is stacked by the door, your notebook is filled with observations, and your camera holds hundreds of photographs documenting the journey. Within the next few days, your attention will shift back to classes, work, deadlines, and daily responsibilities.
Although the environment has changed, the decisions you made throughout the expedition remain fresh in your mind. You recognize that experiences only create value if they influence future performance.
scenarios.decisionPoint: Before fully returning to your normal routine, what do you choose to do first?

options.label: A
options.title: The Reset
options.text: You clean, inspect, and store every piece of equipment. You believe that properly closing one project is the best preparation for the next.

options.label: B
options.title: The Documentation
options.text: You organize your notes, photographs, maps, and observations into a complete record. You believe accurate documentation preserves knowledge that may become valuable later.

options.label: C
options.title: The Reflection
options.text: You deliberately set aside uninterrupted time to evaluate the expedition as a whole. You analyze your decisions, assumptions, successes, and mistakes before drawing conclusions.

options.label: D
options.title: The Application
options.text: You immediately begin identifying ways to apply lessons from the expedition to your academic, professional, or personal goals. You view every experience as training for future challenges.

scenarios.title: The Last Entry
scenarios.narrativeText:
Late that evening, before putting your field journal back on the shelf, you notice one final blank page. You realize this will be the last thing you write about the expedition. Weeks from now, the details will begin to fade, but whatever you choose to record now will likely become the memory that remains.
You pause for a moment, pen in hand.
scenarios.decisionPoint: What do you choose to record?

options.label: A
options.text: You write a practical summary of the expedition—the route you traveled, the equipment that worked, the mistakes you made, and the logistical lessons that will improve future trips.

options.label: B
options.text: You document the evidence you gathered as objectively as possible, organizing your observations so someone else could independently understand and evaluate the site.

options.label: C
options.text: You write about the people you encountered—the researchers, the fisherman, the campers, the farmer—and how each conversation changed your understanding of the landscape.

options.label: D
options.text: You don't focus on the expedition itself. Instead, you write about how the experience changed the way you think, solve problems, and approach uncertainty.
